entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To return to a topic or question later, once you have more information or have had time to think about it.
entries.usage: Very common in American meetings and emails, especially to postpone a question politely: *Let's circle back to that next week*. With a person, it means getting back in touch: *I'll circle back with you on Friday*. Many people see it as corporate jargon, so it sounds empty if you never actually return to the topic.
entries.pattern: circle back to + topic / circle back with + person
examples: We're almost out of time, so let's **circle back** to the budget question next week.
Thanks for the draft. I'll **circle back** once I've had a chance to check the numbers myself.
The senator dodged the question, but the reporter **circled back** to it at the end of the interview.

drill.sentence: I don't have the latest numbers in front of me. Can we {{circle back}} to this on Thursday?
drill.hint: return to it later (American meeting jargon)

entries.related: *follow up* — act on something later, often with a message; *revisit* — more formal, look at a question or decision again; *table* (US) — formally postpone a topic.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: To stop discussing a detailed or sensitive issue in a meeting and talk about it later, separately, with only the people it concerns.
entries.usage: A polite way to keep a meeting on track when two people start going into detail: *Let's take this offline*. Here *offline* has nothing to do with the internet; it means outside the meeting. It is standard in corporate and tech settings, though some people find it a jargon cliché.
entries.pattern: take this / that / it offline
examples: This is getting into the weeds, so let's **take it offline** and finish the agenda.
At the HOA meeting, the chair asked the two neighbors to **take** their parking dispute **offline**.
Rather than debate authorship in front of the whole lab, my advisor **took the conversation offline**.

drill.sentence: You two clearly need more time on the budget numbers. Can you {{take it offline}} so the rest of us can move on?
drill.hint: discuss it separately later with just the people involved

entries.related: *circle back* — return to the topic later, usually with the same group; *park* — set a topic aside for now (*let's park that*); *a sidebar* (US) — a short separate conversation.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have the same understanding of a plan, goal or situation as the other people involved.
entries.usage: Very common at work to check agreement before acting, as in *Just to make sure we're on the same page, the deadline is Friday*. It sounds cooperative, and *we're not on the same page* is a soft way to say that people disagree or misunderstand each other. *Get everyone on the same page* means bring a group to a shared understanding.
entries.pattern: be / get (everyone) on the same page (about something)
examples: Before we start writing the proposal, let's make sure we're all **on the same page** about the main goal.
My partner and I weren't **on the same page** about money, and it caused a lot of fights.
The coach's first job was to get the whole team **on the same page** before the playoffs.

drill.sentence: I'll send a short summary after the call so everyone is {{on the same page}} about next steps.
drill.hint: sharing one understanding

entries.related: *aligned* — corporate word for the same idea (*we're aligned*); *see eye to eye* — agree in opinion, not just share an understanding.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A short, often informal meeting or call where people update each other on progress and coordinate next steps.
entries.usage: Very common in American tech and corporate culture, in speech, chat and calendar invites. *Sync* is also a verb (*Let's sync tomorrow*, *I'll sync up with the data team*). It sounds efficient and casual; in formal writing, say *a brief meeting* or *a short call*.
entries.pattern: have / set up / do a quick sync (with someone); sync (up) with someone
examples: Can we do **a quick sync** after lunch? I want to make sure our slides don't overlap.
I put **a quick sync** on your calendar for Friday to go over the client's feedback.
Our wedding planner wanted **a quick sync** every Monday, which made the whole thing feel like a work project.

drill.sentence: I'm confused about who's handling the launch email. Do you have ten minutes today for {{a quick sync}}?
drill.hint: a short status meeting (office jargon)

entries.related: *a check-in* — similar, often also about how someone is doing; *a stand-up* — a short daily team meeting in software teams; *a huddle* — a very short meeting, often called on the spot.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make brief contact with someone, by talking, calling or messaging, to check how things are going or to share updates.
entries.usage: Common in American business speech and email, as in *I wanted to touch base about the contract*. It sounds friendly and low-pressure, so it is a popular way to open a follow-up email without seeming pushy. Use *with* for the person and *about* or *on* for the topic; the phrase is fixed, so never *touch the base*.
entries.pattern: touch base (with someone) (about / on something)
examples: I just wanted to **touch base** about the reimbursement form I sent last week.
Let's **touch base** on Monday and see where everyone is with the experiments.
I **touched base** with a few old friends while I was back in Chicago.

drill.sentence: A week before the wedding, I'll {{touch base}} with the caterer to confirm the final head count.
drill.hint: make brief contact to confirm details — idiom (not *check in*)

entries.related: *check in (with someone)* — very close, often also about how someone is doing; *reach out* — make contact, often for the first time; *follow up* — contact someone again about something already discussed.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To join a phone or video call, usually a short one that is set up quickly.
entries.usage: Very common in American workplace chat and email since remote work spread. *Hop* makes the call sound quick and easy, so *Can you hop on a call?* is a casual way to suggest talking instead of typing. In formal emails, write *join a call* or *have a call*; you can also *hop on Zoom* or *hop off* a call.
entries.pattern: hop on a (quick) call / Zoom (with someone)
examples: This is hard to explain over Slack. Can you **hop on a call** for five minutes?
I'm at the airport, but I can **hop on a call** before my flight boards.
My grandpa **hops on a video call** with the grandkids every Sunday morning.

drill.sentence: This email thread is going in circles. Can we all {{hop on a call}} at three and sort it out?
drill.hint: quickly join a phone or video conversation (not *jump on* or *get on*)

entries.related: *jump on a call* — same meaning; *get on a call* — more neutral; *set up a call* — plan one for later.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A private meeting between two people, usually a manager and someone who reports to them, often held on a regular schedule.
entries.usage: Standard in American workplaces and research groups, and often written *1:1* in calendars and chat. It works as a noun (*my weekly one-on-one with my advisor*) and as an adjective (*one-on-one meetings*). British English usually says *one-to-one*.
entries.pattern: a (weekly) one-on-one with someone; written 1:1
examples: I have **a one-on-one** with my manager every Tuesday to talk through priorities and blockers.
If you're unhappy with your workload, bring it up in **your one-on-one** rather than in the team meeting.
The new principal scheduled **a one-on-one** with every teacher during her first month.

drill.sentence: After every season, the coach has {{a one-on-one}} with each player to talk about the next year.
drill.hint: a regular private meeting of just two people

mistake.wrong: I have a one-to-one with my boss on Mondays.
mistake.right: I have a one-on-one with my boss on Mondays.
mistake.why: *One-to-one* is the British form; Americans say *one-on-one*.

entries.related: *a check-in* — a shorter, less formal update; *a performance review* — a formal evaluation, usually once or twice a year.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A fixed time when you must leave a meeting or call, whether or not it has finished.
entries.usage: Usually announced at the start so others can plan, as in *Just a heads-up, I have a hard stop at 11*. It sounds professional because you warn people early instead of leaving suddenly. The usual grammar is *have a hard stop at* + time, and a meeting itself can *have a hard stop*.
entries.pattern: have a hard stop at + time
examples: I'm happy to meet, but I have **a hard stop** at 2:30 for a dentist appointment.
The room is booked after us, so we have **a hard stop** at noon.
The panel had **a hard stop** at six, so the moderator cut the Q&A short.

drill.sentence: Just so you know, I have {{a hard stop}} at four because I need to pick up my kids.
drill.hint: a fixed time I must leave

entries.related: *a soft stop* — a preferred end time that can move; *drop off* — leave a call (*I need to drop off*); *run over* — continue past the planned end.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A specific task, agreed in a meeting, that a named person must complete, usually by a set date.
entries.usage: Common in meeting notes, follow-up emails and project tools, usually in the plural: *Here are the action items from today's call*. Each one normally has an owner and a deadline. It sounds organized and businesslike; in casual speech people say *to-dos* or *next steps*.
entries.pattern: the action items from a meeting; an action item for someone
examples: The main **action item** from today's meeting is for Priya to rerun the baseline with the new data.
I'll send out the notes and **action items** by end of day.
The neighborhood association's only **action item** was to email the city about the broken streetlights.

drill.sentence: Can you write up the notes and list the {{action items}}, with an owner and a deadline for each?
drill.hint: concrete tasks people agreed to do afterward

entries.related: *next steps* — more general, less formal; *a deliverable* — a finished result that must be handed in; *a to-do* — informal, any task.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To give your opinion in a discussion or decision, often because your view or expertise matters.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, emails and the news. It suggests your view carries weight, so inviting someone to *weigh in* is a polite way to ask an expert or a senior colleague for input. Use *on* before the topic and *with* before the opinion itself (*She weighed in with a few concerns*).
entries.pattern: weigh in (on something) / weigh in with + opinion
examples: Before we choose a framework, I'd like everyone on the team to **weigh in**.
Several Nobel laureates **weighed in on** the debate over the new funding rules.
My mother-in-law **weighs in on** every decision we make about the kids.

drill.sentence: You've lived in Austin for years, so could you {{weigh in}} on which neighborhood we should look at?
drill.hint: give your opinion, as someone who knows

entries.related: *chime in* — add a comment, more casual and less authoritative; *pipe up* — suddenly start speaking, informal; *have a say* — have the right to influence a decision.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start speaking in a conversation or discussion that is already going on, often by politely interrupting.
entries.usage: Very common in meetings and on calls as a polite request to interrupt: *Can I jump in here?* or *Sorry to jump in, but…*. Inviting others with *Feel free to jump in* tells them they can interrupt you with questions. It sounds friendly and quick; *If I could add something* is the more formal choice.
entries.pattern: Can I jump in (here)? / Sorry to jump in, but … / jump in with + comment
examples: Sorry, can I **jump in** here? I think we're mixing up two different deadlines.
Feel free to **jump in** with questions at any point during the demo.
At dinner, my uncle kept **jumping in** before anyone could finish a sentence.

drill.sentence: Sorry to {{jump in}}, but I think the conference room is only booked until three.
drill.hint: start talking in the middle of someone's turn — phrasal verb (not *cut in* or *butt in*)

entries.related: *chime in* — add a comment, usually without interrupting; *cut in* — interrupt, can sound rude; *butt in* — interrupt rudely, informal.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: To take another person's point as a starting point and develop it further with your own idea.
entries.usage: A cooperative way to take the floor in meetings, seminars and panels: *Just to build on what Maya said, …*. It signals that you agree and are adding something, not correcting anyone, so it helps you enter a discussion without sounding competitive. Use it only when your point really extends theirs; otherwise it sounds like an empty transition.
entries.pattern: build on what someone said / build on someone's point (idea, comment)
examples: To **build on what Sam said**, we could also send the survey to people who canceled last year.
I want to **build on Dr. Kim's point** about staffing, because it affects the night shift too.
Our philosophy professor grades participation, and she rewards students who **build on what others have said**.

drill.sentence: I'd like to {{build on}} what Ana said about the bus routes, because the same problem affects the school schedule.
drill.hint: take her point and develop it further (not *add to*, *expand on* or *piggyback on*)

entries.related: *piggyback on* — same idea, more informal; *to your point* — picks up and supports a point; *expand on* — give more detail on a point.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: A spoken link that connects what you are about to say to the point another person just made, usually to support or extend it.
entries.usage: Very common in American meetings and panel discussions, often with a name: *To Jen's point, …*. It sounds attentive and cooperative, but it is overused, and people notice when the next sentence doesn't really connect to the earlier point. In writing, *as you noted* is more neutral.
entries.pattern: To your point, … / To + name's point, …
examples: **To your point** about the long wait times, we've had three complaints this week alone.
**To Marcus's point**, the cheaper option would also be easier to maintain.
I agree with you. **To your point**, this neighborhood doesn't need another coffee shop; it needs a grocery store.

drill.sentence: {{To your point}}, Kevin, the night shift is already understaffed, so more paperwork would make it worse.
drill.hint: picking up on what you just said, in support (not *as you said* or *like you said*)

entries.related: *building on that* — adds a new idea; *as you said* — plainer, simply refers back; *that's a good point* — praise without adding anything.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To pause and look at the bigger picture of a problem or situation before continuing, instead of focusing on the details in front of you.
entries.usage: Common in meetings when a discussion is stuck in details or going in circles: *Can we take a step back for a second?* It sounds calm and reasonable, and it is a polite way to question the whole approach without attacking anyone. It is often followed by *and ask* or *and look at*.
entries.pattern: take a step back (and ask / look at …)
examples: We've spent an hour on fonts. Let's **take a step back** and ask what the poster actually needs to say.
Before we hire another nurse, let's **take a step back** and look at why so many people are quitting.
When my son and I fight about homework, I try to **take a step back** and figure out what's really bothering him.

drill.sentence: We keep fixing one bug after another. Maybe we should {{take a step back}} and rethink the whole design.
drill.hint: pause and look at the bigger picture — four words (not *zoom out*)

entries.related: *zoom out* — informal, same idea; *the big picture* — the overall situation; *get into the weeds* — the opposite, focus on small details.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To give someone all the recent information they need about a project or situation, so that they know as much as everyone else.
entries.usage: Used when someone joins late, returns from leave or takes over a task: *Can you bring Raj up to speed on the grant?* The person goes between *bring* and *up to speed*, and the topic follows *on*. *Get someone up to speed* is equally common, and *be up to speed* means you already know the latest.
entries.pattern: bring / get someone up to speed (on something)
examples: Lena missed last week's meeting, so I'll **bring her up to speed** on the new schedule.
The night nurse spent fifteen minutes **bringing** the day team **up to speed** on each patient.
When I got back from vacation, my roommate **brought me up to speed** on all the building drama.

drill.sentence: Our new postdoc starts Monday. Could you spend an hour {{bringing her up to speed}} on the project?
drill.hint: giving her all the recent information (not *getting her …*, *catching her up* or *filling her in*)

entries.related: *fill someone in* — tell someone details they missed, more casual; *catch someone up* — same idea, informal; *up to date* — having the latest information.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To start discussing small, technical details, usually more than the situation or the audience needs.
entries.usage: Common in American workplaces, often as a warning or an apology: *Without getting too far into the weeds, …*. It sounds relaxed and self-aware, so it works in most meetings and talks. In formal writing, say *go into technical detail* instead.
entries.pattern: get (too far) into the weeds (on / about something)
examples: I don't want to **get into the weeds**, but the whole delay comes down to one missing permit.
The board meeting **got into the weeds** on parking rules, and we never discussed the budget.
Once my dad starts talking about his golf swing, he **gets into the weeds** fast.

drill.sentence: This talk is for the whole department, so don't {{get into the weeds}} about how the scheduler assigns nodes.
drill.hint: discuss tiny technical points at length (not *go into detail*)

entries.related: *a deep dive* — a detailed look, usually positive; *the big picture* — the overall view, the opposite; *the nitty-gritty* — the practical details.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A thorough, detailed study or discussion of one particular topic, often after a more general overview.
entries.usage: Very common in business, tech and journalism: *do a deep dive into the numbers*, *next week's deep dive on hiring*. It sounds energetic and positive, but it is also standard corporate jargon, so in academic writing prefer *a detailed analysis*. The verb *deep-dive into* exists but sounds even more like jargon.
entries.pattern: do / take a deep dive into (or on) something
examples: Next week's meeting will be **a deep dive into** why so many customers cancel after the first month.
The podcast did **a deep dive into** the history of the Brooklyn Bridge.
Our journal club is doing **a deep dive into** the new sepsis guidelines this Friday.

drill.sentence: We only had time for an overview today, but next week we'll do {{a deep dive}} into the survey results.
drill.hint: a thorough, detailed examination

entries.related: *drill down* — move to finer and finer detail; *an overview* — the opposite, a general summary; *get into the weeds* — go into too much detail.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: Because time is limited; used to explain why you are skipping, shortening or speeding up something.
entries.usage: A polite, slightly formal phrase used by chairs, speakers and teachers, usually at the start of the sentence: *In the interest of time, I'll skip the methods slides*. It makes cutting something sound reasonable rather than rude. *In the interests of time* also exists and is more common in British English.
examples: **In the interest of time**, let's skip the introductions and go straight to the budget.
The judge asked both lawyers, **in the interest of time**, to keep their closing arguments short.
We skipped the museum **in the interest of time** and drove straight to the hotel.

drill.sentence: I'll skip the last three slides {{in the interest of time}}, but they're all in the handout.
drill.hint: because the minutes are limited — fixed phrase (not *to save…* or *for the sake of…*)

entries.related: *for the sake of time* — same, a little less formal; *to save time* — plainer; *in the interest of fairness* — the same pattern with other nouns.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: What you say when you and someone else start speaking at the same moment, to let them speak first.
entries.usage: Extremely common on video calls, where small audio delays make people talk over each other. The usual answer is *No, you go ahead* or *No, please, you go*, and then one person takes the turn. Say it quickly and lightly; it is a reflex, not a real apology.
examples: Oh, **sorry, go ahead**. I didn't realize you were still talking.
The interviewer and I started talking at the same time, so I said, "**Sorry, go ahead**."
At dinner, my sister and I started telling the same story at once. "**Sorry, go ahead**," she said, laughing.

drill.sentence: We both unmuted at the same time. "{{Sorry, go ahead}}," I said, and let her finish her question.
drill.hint: apologize and give her the turn (not *after you* or *you first*)

entries.related: *after you* — lets someone go first, usually through a door; *no, you go* — the usual reply; *talk over someone* — speak at the same time as someone, often rudely.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Asks someone to pause what they are about to say and remember it, because the conversation will come back to it soon.
entries.usage: Used in meetings, classes and conversation when the timing is wrong for a point: *Hold that thought, we'll get to it after the break*. It sounds friendly and shows you value the idea, but only if you really return to it. It is also common in daily life when something interrupts you (*Hold that thought, my phone's ringing*).
examples: **Hold that thought**, Jamal. We'll get to the staffing question right after the break.
Can you **hold that thought**? The baby just woke up, and I'll be right back.
The chemistry teacher asked Ella to **hold that thought** until everyone had finished cleaning up.

drill.sentence: Great question, but {{hold that thought}}: we'll cover it in the second half of the workshop.
drill.hint: keep that idea for a moment; we'll come back to it (not *hang on to that*)

entries.related: *park that* — set a topic aside, more corporate; *put a pin in it* — same, informal and US; *hang on* — wait a moment, more general.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: To have another meeting or appointment already scheduled at the same time, so that you can't attend.
entries.usage: A polite, neutral excuse in American workplaces and schools, because it doesn't say what the other appointment is: *I have a conflict at 3 — could we do 4?* In calendars and email you also see *a scheduling conflict*. This *conflict* has nothing to do with an argument; it is a clash of times.
entries.pattern: have a conflict (at + time / on + day / with + event)
examples: I'd love to come to the talk, but I **have a conflict** at noon. Will there be a recording?
Two board members **had conflicts**, so we moved the vote to next Tuesday.
Thursday doesn't work for me; I **have a conflict** with my daughter's school play.

drill.sentence: Can we move our call to Friday? I just realized I {{have a conflict}} on Thursday afternoon.
drill.hint: already have another appointment at that time — polite calendar phrase (not *have plans*)

entries.related: *a scheduling conflict* — the full form, more formal; *a clash* — more British for the same idea; *double-booked* — two appointments at the same time, often by mistake.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To move a meeting or event to a later time or date.
entries.usage: Common in speech, chat and email: *Can we push our call back to 3?* Use *to* for the new time and *by* for the amount of delay (*push it back by a week*). For an earlier time, Americans say *move it up*; British speakers usually say *bring it forward*.
entries.pattern: push something back (to + time / by + amount)
examples: The client's flight was delayed, so we **pushed the meeting back** to four o'clock.
Can we **push** our one-on-one **back** a week? I'm buried in grading.
The city **pushed back** the opening of the new library until spring.

drill.sentence: My train is running late. Would you mind if we {{pushed the meeting back}} half an hour?
drill.hint: shifted it to a later start (not *moved* or *postponed*)

entries.related: *postpone* — more formal, often with no new time yet; *move up* — the opposite, to an earlier time; *reschedule* — change the time in either direction.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To suggest an idea casually and tentatively, without strongly recommending it, so that others can react to it.
entries.usage: Common in brainstorming and meetings, usually as *Just to throw it out there, …* or *I'll throw this out there: …*. It lowers the pressure: you signal that the idea may not work and that you won't mind if it's rejected. It is mostly spoken; in an email, *one option might be* is more neutral.
entries.pattern: throw it / this / something out there
examples: This might be a crazy idea, but I'll **throw it out there**: what if we hold the retreat online?
Just to **throw something out there**, we could split the night shifts between the two units.
I'm just **throwing it out there**, but we could rent a cabin instead of a hotel this year.

drill.sentence: I'm not sure it would work, but let me {{throw this out there}}: what if we let the kids plan the menu?
drill.hint: offer this idea casually, just to see how people react (not *float this* or *suggest this*)

entries.related: *float an idea* — suggest it tentatively, a bit more formal; *spitball* — brainstorm loosely, informal US; *for what it's worth* — offers an opinion modestly.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The specific actions that people agree to take after a meeting or decision, in order to move the work forward.
entries.usage: Almost always plural, and very common at the end of meetings and in follow-up emails: *So what are the next steps?* It is also a standard heading in meeting notes, and a meeting that ends without clear next steps is a typical complaint. Compared with *action items*, it is less formal and does not always name an owner.
examples: Before we hang up, let's agree on **next steps**: who contacts the vendor, and who updates the budget?
The doctor explained the **next steps**: more blood work, then a follow-up visit in two weeks.
After the interview, I asked the recruiter about **next steps** in the hiring process.

drill.sentence: Thanks, everyone. I'll email a short summary with {{next steps}} and who owns each one.
drill.hint: the actions agreed for afterward (not *action items* or *to-dos*)

entries.related: *action items* — specific tasks with owners, more formal; *the way forward* — the general plan, more formal; *a follow-up* — what happens after a meeting or event.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To reach a shared agreement with others about a plan, priority or decision before acting on it.
entries.usage: Typical American corporate jargon: *Let's align on the timeline before we talk to the client*. Many people find it vague or mock it as a buzzword, so outside large companies *agree on* or *decide on* sounds more natural. Related forms are *get aligned*, *we're aligned* and *alignment*.
entries.pattern: align on + plan / priorities / next steps (with someone)
examples: Before we present to the client, we need to **align on** a single price and stick to it.
The two departments still haven't **aligned on** who owns the new patient portal.
My wife joked that we should **align on** dinner plans as if it were a board meeting.

drill.sentence: Let's {{align on}} the main message before the press release goes out, so nobody contradicts it.
drill.hint: reach a shared position about — corporate jargon (not *agree on*)

entries.related: *agree on* — plain and neutral; *be on the same page* — informal, share the same understanding; *buy-in* — support for a plan from the people who must carry it out.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: On a phone or video call: your microphone is switched off, so nobody can hear what you're saying.
entries.usage: One of the most common sentences of remote work, said kindly when someone speaks without being heard, or typed in the chat. *I think you're on mute* sounds softer, and the usual answer is *Sorry, I was on mute*. *You're muted* means the same.
examples: Sarah, **you're on mute**. We can see your lips moving, but there's no sound.
I talked for two full minutes before someone typed "**you're on mute**" in the chat.
My grandma waved at the screen while we all shouted, "Grandma, **you're on mute**!"

drill.sentence: Hi, Dev? We can't hear you. I think {{you're on mute}}; the microphone icon is crossed out.
drill.hint: your microphone is switched off (not the adjective *muted*)

entries.related: *you're muted* — same meaning; *unmute* — switch the microphone back on; *you're breaking up* — your audio keeps cutting out.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To discuss a problem, plan or decision carefully and step by step, in order to understand it fully or reach a decision.
entries.usage: Common at work and in personal life, with a patient, supportive tone: *Let's talk it through before you decide*. With a pronoun, the object goes in the middle (*talk it through*); with a longer noun, both orders work (*talk through the options*). *Talk someone through something* means guide a person step by step.
entries.pattern: talk it through / talk through + noun (with someone)
examples: I'm not sure about the job offer yet. Can we **talk it through** over dinner?
Before the surgery, the anesthesiologist **talked through** each step with the patient's family.
The team **talked through** three ways to fix the delay and settled on the cheapest one.

drill.sentence: Don't decide about the apartment tonight. Sleep on it, and we'll {{talk it through}} tomorrow morning.
drill.hint: examine it together point by point (not *… it over*, *discuss it* or *go over it*)

entries.related: *talk something over* — discuss, often a personal decision; *walk someone through* — explain step by step; *hash out* — discuss until disagreements are settled.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: In American English, to postpone discussing a topic or proposal until a later time, often without setting a date.
entries.usage: Used in formal meetings, committees and boards: *Let's table this until next month*, or *The motion was tabled*. In British English *table* means the opposite, to put a topic forward for discussion, which can cause real confusion in international teams. With a mixed group, say *postpone* or *put on hold* instead.
entries.pattern: table a discussion / motion / proposal (until …)
examples: We're out of time, so let's **table** the parking discussion until the next board meeting.
The faculty senate voted to **table** the proposal on grading changes.
My husband and I **tabled** the question of getting a dog until after the move.

drill.sentence: We clearly need more data on costs, so I move that we {{table}} this item until the June meeting.
drill.hint: set aside for now, US sense (not *postpone*, *defer* or *shelve*)

entries.related: *postpone* — neutral, understood everywhere; *shelve* — set aside, often for a long time; *park* — informal, set a topic aside for now.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To set an idea or topic aside for now, with the intention of returning to it later.
entries.usage: Common in meetings and workshops, especially *Let's park that for now*. Some facilitators keep a *parking lot*: a list of parked topics on a whiteboard or in shared notes. It sounds friendly and efficient, but people notice if parked items never come back.
entries.pattern: park that / this / the idea (for now)
examples: Good point, but it's a bigger question. Let's **park** it for now and come back to it after lunch.
We **parked** the idea of a second location until sales pick up.
My sister and I agreed to **park** the argument about Mom's birthday until we'd both calmed down.

drill.sentence: That's a great idea for next year's festival, but can we {{park}} it for now and focus on this one?
drill.hint: set it aside temporarily — one word (not *table* or *shelve*)

entries.related: *put a pin in it* — same, informal US; *table* (US) — postpone, more formal; *a parking lot* — a list of parked topics.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stop discussing a topic for now and agree to come back to it later.
entries.usage: Very common in American meetings and everyday talk: *Let's put a pin in that*. It sounds light and friendly, though some people treat it as a corporate cliché. It is more casual than *table* and very close to *park*.
entries.pattern: put a pin in it / that / this
examples: That's a really good question about pricing. Can we **put a pin in it** and come back after the demo?
We **put a pin in** the kitchen remodel until we know whether I'm getting the job in Denver.
The coach **put a pin in** the new playbook until the injured players were back.

drill.sentence: I don't want to lose your idea about the reunion. Let's {{put a pin in}} it and talk after the kids are asleep.
drill.hint: mark it to return to later — four-word idiom (not *park* or *table*)

entries.related: *park something* — same, also common in British English; *table* (US) — postpone, more formal; *hold that thought* — asks one person to pause their point.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: In a discussion, to add your own idea to what someone else has just said, using their point as a starting point.
entries.usage: Common in American meetings: *Can I piggyback on that?* or *Just to piggyback on what Lisa said, …*. It sounds casual and team-minded, and some people find it a little cute; *build on* is the neutral choice. In relaxed speech you also hear *piggyback off (of) that*.
entries.pattern: piggyback on that / on what someone said
examples: Can I **piggyback on** that? Besides the price, the delivery time is also a problem.
Just to **piggyback on** what the charge nurse said, we also need more wheelchairs on this floor.
At the PTA meeting, every parent seemed to **piggyback on** the last comment about the bus schedule.

drill.sentence: If I could {{piggyback on}} Tom's point about parking, the same rule should apply to bikes.
drill.hint: use what he said as a starting point — informal (not *build on* or *add to*)

entries.related: *build on* — neutral, same idea; *to your point* — picks up and supports a point; *echo* — repeat and agree with what someone said.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: To let each person in a meeting or class speak in turn, usually to introduce themselves or give a short update or opinion.
entries.usage: Common at the start of meetings, workshops and classes: *Let's go around the room and do quick introductions*. People say it on video calls too, where there is no room; with a small group at one table, *go around the table* is also common. Adding a limit (*thirty seconds each*) keeps it from taking too long.
entries.pattern: go around the room (and + verb)
examples: Since we have a few new faces, let's **go around the room** and have everyone say their name and role.
At the start of every lab meeting, we **go around the room** and share one win from the week.
The therapist **went around the room** and asked each person in the group how their week had been.

drill.sentence: We have ten minutes left, so let's quickly {{go around the room}}; everyone gets one sentence about their biggest concern.
drill.hint: let each person speak in turn (not *… the table*)

entries.related: *go around the table* — same, for a group at one table; *a round-robin* — everyone takes a turn; *a roundtable* — an informal discussion among equals.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To return to the main topic of a discussion, or to the original plan or schedule, after a distraction or delay.
entries.usage: In meetings it is a polite way to end a side conversation: *Let's get back on track*. In projects and personal life it means recovering after falling behind (*The project is back on track*). The topic or plan often follows *with* (*get back on track with the budget*).
entries.pattern: get / be back on track (with something)
examples: We've drifted into vacation stories. Let's **get back on track** and finish the agenda.
After two weeks of holiday cookies, I'm trying to **get back on track** with my running.
The new manager helped the delayed construction project **get back on track** by spring.

drill.sentence: I know last night's game was wild, but we only have twenty minutes, so let's {{get back on track}} with the budget.
drill.hint: return to the main subject after a distraction

entries.related: *get sidetracked* — move away from the main topic; *stay on topic* — avoid distractions; *off track* — away from the plan or topic.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To examine something in more and more detail, moving from a general level to specific parts or data.
entries.usage: Common in business, data analysis and tech: *drill down into the numbers by region*. It suggests a step-by-step move from a summary to the details, often in a dashboard or spreadsheet. For people or ideas, *dig deeper* is the more conversational choice.
entries.pattern: drill down into something (by + category)
examples: Sales look flat overall, but when you **drill down into** the data by store, two locations are growing fast.
The auditors **drilled down into** every expense over five hundred dollars.
The hospital **drilled down into** its readmission numbers and found that most came from a single unit.

drill.sentence: The yearly average hides a lot. If you {{drill down into}} the monthly numbers, you'll see the summer spike.
drill.hint: examine in finer and finer detail (not *dig into*)

entries.related: *dig deeper* — investigate further, more conversational; *a deep dive* — a detailed study of one topic; *break down* — split totals into parts (*break down by age*).

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To keep talking without really understanding each other, because each person is answering a different point or using words differently.
entries.usage: Used to describe a frustrating discussion, often by someone trying to fix it: *I think we're talking past each other*. It is a neutral, non-blaming way to say that a disagreement is partly a misunderstanding. A related form is *talk past someone* (*I felt he was talking past me*).
entries.pattern: talk past each other / one another
examples: I think we're **talking past each other**: you mean the launch date, and I mean the delivery date.
The two doctors kept **talking past each other**, because one meant risk to the patient and the other meant risk to the hospital.
My parents argue for hours, but they're really just **talking past each other**.

drill.sentence: Wait, we keep {{talking past each other}}. When you say "small," do you mean the budget or the team?
drill.hint: responding to different points without noticing (not *misunderstanding …*)

entries.related: *at cross-purposes* — misunderstanding because each side means something different; *go around in circles* — keep discussing without progress; *see eye to eye* — agree.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To keep arguing about something without deciding, or to keep changing your mind between two options.
entries.usage: It covers both a debate between people (*We went back and forth with the landlord for weeks*) and one person's indecision (*I've been going back and forth on whether to apply*). Use *on* or *about* for the topic. It sounds neutral, often a little tired.
entries.pattern: go back and forth (with someone) (on / about something)
examples: We **went back and forth on** the title for weeks before we finally picked one.
I've been **going back and forth about** whether to sell the car or keep it.
The two hospitals **went back and forth** for months over who would pay for the new scanner.

drill.sentence: My sister has been {{going back and forth}} on the two job offers, and now she has to decide by Friday.
drill.hint: changing her mind again and again (not *flip-flopping*)

entries.related: *flip-flop* — change position repeatedly, critical; *be torn between* — unable to choose; *haggle* — argue about a price.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: I agree with and support the suggestion or opinion that someone has just given.
entries.usage: It comes from formal meeting procedure, where a motion needs a *second*, but it is now common in everyday meetings and conversation. *I second that* is more direct; *I'd second that* sounds a little softer. In casual speech people often just say *Seconded!*, sometimes jokingly.
examples: Mark suggested ending every meeting five minutes early, and **I'd second that**; we all need the break.
"We should order Thai food tonight." "**I'd second that**."
Several reviews praise the bakery's sourdough, and **I'd second that**: it's the best in town.

drill.sentence: Jen just proposed that we cancel the Friday call during the summer, and {{I'd second that}}.
drill.hint: I would formally support her proposal (not *I agree*)

entries.related: *I'm with you* — informal agreement; *seconded* — very short and casual; *I'd echo that* — repeat and agree with a point.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To let someone with more knowledge, experience or authority make a decision or judgment, instead of insisting on your own view.
entries.usage: Polite and fairly formal, common in meetings, panels and medicine: *I'll defer to Dr. Ruiz on that*. It shows respect and modesty, and it is also a graceful way to avoid a question outside your field. Without *to*, *defer* means postpone (*defer payment*).
entries.pattern: defer to someone (on something) / defer to someone's judgment
examples: I'm not a lawyer, so on the contract question I'll **defer to** Sarah.
The young resident **deferred to** the senior surgeon's judgment, even though she had doubts.
When it comes to wine, I always **defer to** my brother-in-law.

drill.sentence: On the statistics, I'd {{defer to}} Priya; she knows those methods much better than I do.
drill.hint: let her judgment decide — formal (not *leave it to*)

entries.related: *leave it to someone* — let them decide, more casual; *yield to* — give way, often under pressure; *weigh in* — the opposite, give your own opinion.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To attend a meeting, class or session as an observer, without taking a full or official part in it.
entries.usage: Common at work and in universities: *Do you mind if I sit in on your lecture?* Asking to sit in is a polite way to learn or observe, and the host can easily say no. Note the two prepositions: *sit in on* + the event.
entries.pattern: sit in on + meeting / class / session
examples: As a new manager, I asked if I could **sit in on** a few of the senior team's meetings.
Prospective students can **sit in on** a class before they apply.
With the patient's permission, the medical student **sat in on** the consultation.

drill.sentence: Our intern would love to {{sit in on}} the client call tomorrow, just to listen and take notes.
drill.hint: attend as a quiet observer (not *listen in on*)

entries.related: *audit* (US) — attend a university course without credit; *listen in (on)* — listen, sometimes secretly; *shadow someone* — follow a person at work to learn their job.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To meet again as a group after a break or at a later time, to continue the same meeting or discussion.
entries.usage: Used in courts, committees and boards, and in work emails: *Let's take a ten-minute break and reconvene at 2:15*. In everyday meetings it sounds a bit official, which can help when you want a clear plan; casual alternatives are *pick this up again* and *meet again*. Usually the group is the subject, but a chair can also *reconvene the meeting*.
examples: Let's take a fifteen-minute break and **reconvene** at three to finish the review.
The judge announced that court would **reconvene** on Monday morning.
The book club agreed to **reconvene** in January, after the holidays.

drill.sentence: We clearly need the lab results before we decide, so let's {{reconvene}} next Thursday once they're in.
drill.hint: meet again as a group — formal (not *regroup*)

entries.related: *regroup* — gather again, often to rethink a plan; *adjourn* — end or pause a meeting; *convene* — call or hold a formal meeting.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To continue past the time when a meeting, class or event was supposed to end.
entries.usage: Common as an apology or a warning near the end of a meeting: *Sorry, we're running over*, or *I don't want to run over*. Add the amount with *by* (*we ran over by twenty minutes*). *Run long* and *go over (time)* mean the same.
entries.pattern: run over (by + amount)
examples: The meeting **ran over** by half an hour, so I missed my train.
Sorry, I know we're **running over**. Just one more slide.
Our parent-teacher conference **ran over**, and the next family was waiting in the hallway.

drill.sentence: I have to pick up my son at five, so please don't let the review {{run over}} this time.
drill.hint: go past its planned end (not *run long*, *go over* or *drag on*)

entries.related: *run long* — same, informal; *drag on* — continue too long and become boring; *wrap up* — finish a meeting.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: To end a meeting earlier than scheduled, so that people get the remaining minutes for other things.
entries.usage: A friendly American workplace phrase, said by the person running a meeting: *I'll give you fifteen minutes back*. It treats time as a gift, so it sounds considerate, though some people find it a corporate cliché. People also say *Enjoy your ten minutes back!*
entries.pattern: give someone + (amount of) time + back
examples: We covered everything on the agenda, so I'll **give you ten minutes back**.
The professor ended class early and said she was **giving us twenty minutes back** to study for Friday's exam.
The webinar host wrapped up early and **gave everyone fifteen minutes back** before lunch.

drill.sentence: That's all I had for today, so I'll {{give you some time back}}. Have a great weekend!
drill.hint: end the meeting early as a favor to you (not *let you go early*)

entries.related: *let people go early* — plainer; *wrap up early* — finish ahead of schedule; *be respectful of someone's time* — avoid wasting people's time.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A short daily team meeting, often about fifteen minutes, where each person says what they did, what they will do next, and what is blocking them.
entries.usage: It comes from agile software teams, where people stood to keep the meeting short, and it is now common in other offices and labs too. The spelling varies: *standup* or *stand-up*. For the daily meeting, people often drop the article: *at standup*, *in standup*.
entries.pattern: at / in standup; the daily standup
examples: At **standup** this morning, I mentioned that I'm blocked until the vendor sends the new API keys.
Our clinic started a five-minute **standup** each morning to review the day's patients.
My roommate's **standup** is at nine sharp, so he joins from the kitchen in his pajamas.

drill.sentence: Our team has {{a standup}} every morning at 9:15: what you did yesterday, what's next, and what's blocking you.
drill.hint: a short daily progress meeting (not *a huddle* or *a check-in*)

entries.related: *a quick sync* — a short meeting set up when needed; *a huddle* — a very brief meeting, common in health care; *a retro* — a team meeting about what went well and badly.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A meeting for everyone in a company, department or organization, usually led by senior leaders to share news and plans.
entries.usage: Common in American companies and universities, often shortened: *There's an all-hands at noon*. Because it usually means important news, a sudden all-hands can make people nervous. The phrase comes from ships, where *all hands* means the whole crew.
entries.pattern: an / the all-hands (meeting)
examples: The CEO called **an all-hands meeting** to announce the merger before it hit the news.
There's **an all-hands** at noon, so let's push our sync to two.
The dean's office holds **an all-hands meeting** each semester for faculty and staff.

drill.sentence: Every employee is expected at Friday's {{all-hands}}, where the founders will present the new strategy.
drill.hint: a meeting for the whole company (not *town hall*)

entries.related: *a town hall* — a large meeting with open questions to leaders; *a standup* — a short daily team meeting; *all hands on deck* — everyone must help.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: On a phone or video call: your audio keeps cutting out, so I can only hear parts of what you're saying.
entries.usage: Said politely when someone's connection is bad, usually with a request: *You're breaking up — can you say that again?* It describes the signal, not the person, so it isn't rude. *You're cutting out* means the same, and *you froze* is used when the video stops.
examples: Sorry, Ahmed, **you're breaking up**. Could you repeat the last part about the budget?
I'm getting into the elevator, so I might start **breaking up**. I'll call you right back.
Mom, **you're breaking up** — are you driving through the canyon again?

drill.sentence: Hello? {{You're breaking up}}; I only caught every third word. Maybe try moving closer to the router.
drill.hint: your audio keeps dropping (not *cutting out*)

entries.related: *you're cutting out* — same; *you're frozen* — your video has stopped; *you're on mute* — your microphone is off.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To leave a phone call or online meeting before it ends, or to be disconnected from it.
entries.usage: Common in remote work: *I have to drop off at 10:30* warns others politely, and *I'm going to drop off now* is a quick exit. It also describes accidental disconnection (*I think Tom dropped off*). In formal settings, *I need to leave the call* is the plain alternative.
entries.pattern: drop off (the call) (at + time)
examples: I have to **drop off** at eleven for another meeting, so please send me the notes.
Half the parents **dropped off** the school's Zoom meeting before the Q&A started.
Grandpa **dropped off the call** again; I think his Wi-Fi is acting up.

drill.sentence: I have another meeting, so I'm going to {{drop off}} now, but Leah will stay on and take notes.
drill.hint: leave the call early (not *hop off*, *jump off*, *sign off* or *log off*)

entries.related: *hop off* — same, informal US; *hop on a call* — the opposite, join; *get cut off* — be disconnected by accident.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To take a short break, of about five minutes, from work, a meeting or an activity.
entries.usage: Common in long meetings, rehearsals, film sets and sports practice, usually as a suggestion: *Let's take five*. It is casual and friendly, the number isn't strict, and *take ten* works the same way. In a formal agenda, write *a short break*.
examples: We've been at this for two hours. Let's **take five** and grab some coffee.
The director told the cast to **take five** while the crew fixed the lighting.
Halfway up the trail, the kids begged us to **take five** in the shade.

drill.sentence: Everyone looks exhausted. Why don't we {{take five}} and grab some water before the last item?
drill.hint: pause for a few minutes — two words, the second is a number

entries.related: *take a breather* — rest briefly, informal; *a bio break* — office jargon for a short restroom break; *call it a day* — stop working completely.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A very broad, high-level overview of a situation or project, without details.
entries.usage: American business jargon, based on the view from a plane: *Let me give you the 30,000-foot view*. It is useful before going into detail, but many people find it a cliché, so *a high-level overview* or *the big picture* is safer with academics or clients. The opposite is being *in the weeds*.
examples: Before we get into the numbers, let me give you **the 30,000-foot view** of where the project stands.
My financial adviser started with **a 30,000-foot view**: spend less than you earn, and invest the rest.
The new principal asked for **a 30,000-foot view** of the school's problems before visiting each classroom.

drill.sentence: Don't give the board every detail; they just want {{a 30,000-foot view}} of how the year went.
drill.hint: a very broad overview, as if seen from a plane (not *the big picture* or *bird's-eye …*)

entries.related: *the big picture* — the overall situation, neutral; *high-level* — general, without detail; *a bird's-eye view* — a broad view from above.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: To avoid wasting other people's time, for example by starting and ending meetings on time and keeping requests short.
entries.usage: A polite American workplace phrase, often used by the person running a meeting: *I want to be respectful of everyone's time, so let's stop here*. It can also soften a request or an exit (*I'll be respectful of your time and keep this short*). Some people hear it as a polite formula; *I know you're busy* is plainer.
entries.pattern: be respectful of someone's / everyone's time
examples: I want to **be respectful of everyone's time**, so let's end here and finish the rest by email.
Thanks for meeting with me. I'll **be respectful of your time** and keep this to fifteen minutes.
Our pediatrician is great: she's always **respectful of our time** and rarely keeps us waiting.

drill.sentence: I know you all have a long drive home, so I'll {{be respectful of your time}} and keep my toast short.
drill.hint: avoid wasting your minutes (not *be brief*)

entries.related: *value someone's time* — same idea, slightly warmer; *give someone time back* — end a meeting early; *keep it short* — plain and casual.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To guide a discussion so that it stays focused, everyone can contribute, and the group reaches its goal, usually without pushing your own opinion.
entries.usage: Common in workshops, classes, research groups and community meetings; the person is the *facilitator*. A facilitator manages the process (time, turns, focus) more than the content, which is the difference from leading or chairing. In casual speech, *run* or *lead the discussion* is more common.
entries.pattern: facilitate a / the discussion (between / among people)
examples: Ana will **facilitate the discussion** today, so she'll keep us on time and make sure everyone gets a turn.
The library hired a trained mediator to **facilitate a discussion** between neighbors about the new dog park.
In my seminar, each student has to **facilitate the discussion** of one reading during the semester.

drill.sentence: We need someone neutral to {{facilitate the discussion}}, so that both teams feel heard and we actually reach a decision.
drill.hint: guide the conversation fairly (not *moderate* or *lead* it)

entries.related: *moderate* — run a debate or panel, often deciding who speaks; *chair a meeting* — lead a formal meeting; *a facilitator* — the person who facilitates.
